memory_candidates.content: When a bash script must invoke a command that regenerates its own on-disk (deployed) copy while it is still executing, the reliable mitigation is to wrap EVERYTHING from that call through the file's true EOF inside one top-level function, defined in full (and therefore fully parsed/consumed by bash before any of it runs) and invoked as the file's last physical statement with nothing after it. A partial wrap that closes before EOF re-opens the identical hazard a few hundred lines later. This generalizes cleanly to any 'a subprocess rewrites the currently-executing script' scenario, not just deploy engines.

A lint that must verify a bash function's true closing brace in a codebase full of jq '{...}' single-quoted program literals should NOT use character-level brace-counting -- literal { and } inside quoted strings corrupt the count. Instead, adopt (and check for) the convention of a LONE, UNINDENTED closing brace alone on its own line as the function's true end marker (paired with 'do not re-indent the wrapped body' at authoring time). This sidesteps needing a real shell parser for a structural lint.

When building a deterministic regression harness for a 'file rewritten mid-read' bash hazard using a prepended byte-shifting banner: (1) avoid banner sizes that are exact multiples of common internal read-buffer sizes (e.g. 64KB) -- such sizes can coincidentally re-align the corrupted byte stream onto a safe parse boundary and produce a false pre-fix PASS; prefer a non-round size. (2) Reset the target file to a pristine copy before EVERY test case that rewrites it -- a prior case's leftover rewritten copy compounds into the next case's byte offsets in an uncontrolled way, making results depend on suite ordering rather than the mechanism under test.
